Multi-tenant ERP · client design · 31 August 2026 · revision 4

Back Office Design System

One product, two rooms. The Counter stays what it is — a task-first till built for a queue, daylight and a dead radio. Everything else is a back office: a light, modern SaaS overview — white cards on a soft canvas, pill tabs across the top, delta pills, one violet accent — where every page answers its own question in the first screenful, every chart is chosen for the question it answers, and the numbers say what they are not.

Illustrative figures. Tenant #1 has not traded (Q21, answered 25 Aug 2026). Every number in the mockups is invented to sit near the FY1 model — flagship ≈ GH₵220k/month at 40% ramp — so the layouts are tested against plausible magnitudes. None of it is data. "GH₵", "Flagship", "Contractor" are tenant #1's own words rendered from configuration, never product copy (§8.9).

1 · The split: a till and an office

The current shell offers thirteen destinations in one segmented control designed for a cashier's thumb. Nine of those destinations are not counter work. They are read at a desk, on a tablet propped on a stand, or on the founder's phone in a haulier's yard — scanned, not operated. They need a different room.

Room 1 · unchanged

Counter

Task-first. Catalogue, cart, tender, receipt. Bottom-anchored cart dock, 56px taps, never unmounted. The device's own sales list (Sales) and the two outbox writers that work offline — Adjust and Receive — stay reachable from here as sheets, because they are done at the counter with the radio off.

Room 2 · this document

Back office

Overview-first. Pill tabs across the top, a sync chip, white cards on a soft canvas, a 12-column content grid. Home is a dashboard composed from the session's capabilities. Reports, Stock, Credit, Buying, Suppliers, On the road, Decisions, Books each become a page with a summary strip above its detail.

Who lands where

Role (tenant #1 template)Opens intoDashboard composition
Outlet staffCounterNo back office. Sales list and stock lookup only.
Outlet managerCounter, with a door to the OfficeMy outlet: today's takings, cash vs credit, low stock here, deliveries expected, my open decisions.
Regional managerBack officeMy region: sales by outlet, stock alerts by outlet, haulage in flight, distribution cost for the region.
Head of operations / founderBack officeThe network: everything below, scoped network: true.
AccountsBack office → BooksCredit exposure and ageing, posting exceptions, trial balance status, reconciliation, payroll register.

Composition is by capability, not role name — a tile appears when the session holds the permission its query needs (report.view.*, credit.view, gl.view…). Roles are tenant-editable, so a tenant that gives its regional managers gl.view simply sees the ledger tiles arrive. No if (role === …), anywhere.

2 · Shell anatomy

Three fixed elements, then the page. The office deliberately shares nothing visual with the counter: the counter is blue on daylight grey with 56px targets and a bottom cart dock; the office is Inter on a soft lavender-grey canvas with white 18px-radius cards, pill tabs and soft shadows. A person should never mistake one room for the other.

  1. Top bar — the tenant's mark and name on the left (data, never chrome); a row of pill tabs in the centre — Dashboard, then every destination the session's capabilities allow, in rail order; on the right the sync chip (the same four-state status component as the counter, wearing the office's colours) and a round button back to the counter that carries the cart's line count.
  2. Scope, always on screen — every money tile carries the scope chip: Whole organisation · 1 location versus Your 3 locations only. An outlet manager's total and the founder's total look identical as figures and mean different things.
  3. Content grid — 12 columns, 16px gutters, `grid-auto-flow: dense` so a tile a session cannot see leaves no hole. Stat cards span 3, the analytics hero spans 9, the right column spans 3 across two rows.

Offline in the office. Strictly-online pages (Credit, Buying, Suppliers, Decisions, Books) do not render a stale figure. When the radio is off they show the last answer with a wall-clock age and a disabled action row — never a spinner, never a blank. Every tile also stamps its own As at hh:mm in its footer.

3 · The dashboard

The home page answers the founder's questions in order: Did we sell? Did we get paid? Are we the business in the model? What needs me? Where is the money by place? Will we run out? Each stat card is a title, a delta pill, one large figure and one caption. The one chart that earns width is revenue per business day with its 7-day average and the range's own average as a dashed reference. Nothing needs a hover to be read.

The design mockup (docs/design/mockups/office-dashboard.html), rendered at 1280 and iterated four times. Illustrative figures near the FY1 model. Three charts here are ahead of the API and are shown so the page is designed for its full shape: gross margin by category, cash vs credit by week, and the on-the-road panel.

The real thing — features/office/Dashboard.tsx rendered with app.css and mocked answers in the server's shapes (test currency ¤; tenant #1 has not traded). Layout is rows, not a 12-column auto-flow: each row divides its width among the tiles the session can actually see, so a missing tile leaves no hole and nothing hugs the left. Twelve tiles, one query per report shared between them. Week on week compares full weeks and marks the partial one with *; the basket is drawn as columns so a closed day is a gap, not a dash.

Dark scheme, from the same tokens re-toned for the dark surface — never inverted. Every pill's ink is checked at 4.5:1 against its own tint and every chart series at 3:1 against the card, in both schemes, by tests/design-tokens.test.ts.

4 · Page-by-page visuals

Every page follows the same skeleton — summary strip → one primary visual → the table → the caveats — and picks its primary visual by the job the data does. The table is never optional: it is the accessible view, the print view, and the thing an accountant actually trusts.

Reports — periods, comparisons, charts, CSV

The office Reports page (features/office/Reports.tsx), rendered from the same mocked answers. What makes it a report rather than a table dump: a period a person chooses (7 / 28 / 90 / 365 days or two dates) and, always, the same period before it, so every headline carries a change; one question per card in the right form — change over time, ranking, composition, honest absence; and a Download CSV behind every table, written with the canonical ungrouped money string because the accountant opens it in a spreadsheet. Below the fold: stock on hand (largest quantities, all lines in the CSV) and haulage by carrier.

Decisions deliberately has no chart: a conflict's three values side by side, each with its provenance, is the visual; colour on the proposals is categorical identity, not judgement.

5 · Visual rules that hold on every page

  1. Summary before detail. The stat strip answers the page's question; the visual explains it; the table proves it.
  2. null is never zero. An unavailable ratio renders the word Unavailable in the wait colour with the server's reason. A floor is labelled "floor". A nested group subtotal is indented and never summed. This is the single rule most likely to be broken by a charting library's defaults — which is one reason there is no charting library.
  3. Scope is always on screen. The scope chip is sticky. A total row is named for what it contains ("Your 3 locations", "Whole network").
  4. Staleness is a state, not an error (§8.4). Every server-read page shows wall-clock age when offline, and disables writes rather than hiding them.
  5. One axis per chart. No pies. No dual axes. No rainbow. Two measures of different scale get two charts. Share is a stacked bar with direct labels, not a donut.
  6. Colour never carries meaning alone. Status hues (ok / wait / attn) always pair with an icon or a word; series hues always pair with a direct label or a legend. Text is never set in a series colour.
  7. Series colour follows the entity. A location keeps its hue across filters and pages. Beyond four series, fold to "Other" or facet into small multiples.
  8. Tabular numerals everywhere digits align. Money right-aligned, minor-unit scale from the pack, currency label from the pack, negative as a leading minus — never parentheses in the UI (the accountant's export may use them).
  9. Touch still counts. Office pages are used on the same tablets: 44px minimum targets, row taps open a detail sheet, hover is an enhancement.
  10. Empty states design for the future shape. One trading location today, twenty-five in FY10 — the sales-by-location card is laid out for the list it will hold and says so, instead of collapsing to a lonely bar.

6 · Tokens, type and chart palette

The office has its own palette in apps/web/src/app.css (the --o-* tokens), defined for both schemes at the top of the stylesheet so the contrast test sees them. The counter's tokens are untouched.

Office surfaces and inks

canvas
card
text
muted
violet · accent
mint · good, series 1
amber · warning
red · attention
blue · info

Pills are ink-on-tint pairs (--o-mint-text on --o-mint-tint …), each checked at 4.5:1 in light and dark. Status hues are never a chart series beyond mint.

Chart series

--chart-1 mint
--chart-2 violet
--chart-3 amber
--chart-4 magenta
--chart-target

Fixed order, never cycled. Series 1 and 2 clear 3:1 on the card in both schemes (tested). The colour-vision separation of this set was reasoned from hue distance (mint/violet/amber are far apart on the deutan axis) rather than machine-validated — the palette validator was unavailable in this session; every chart carries direct labels or a legend regardless.

Type

The office sets Inter — the face the reference uses — self-hosted as a latin subset (400/500/600/700, 100 KB, precached with the office chunk) with the system stack as fallback. 13.5px base, 15px card titles, 28px figures at 600 with −0.02em tracking, 11.5px pills. The counter keeps the system stack at 17px: it is read at arm's length, offline, and never loads a font file.

Motion and surfaces

Cards: 18px radius, 1px hairline plus a two-layer shadow at 4% alpha. Tabs and pills: fully rounded. No glass, no backdrop filters (compositor cost on these GPUs). Press feedback is the counter's .pressable transform, reused.

7 · What is built, and what is next

  1. Two rooms, one app — Shell.tsx keeps the counter mounted and hidden behind features/office/OfficeShell.tsx; room.ts offers the office only to sessions holding an office capability. Lazy chunk, 1.5 KB gz.
  2. Top-tab office shell — pill tabs in rail order, gated by capability; sync chip; counter button with cart count; tenant mark and name when known.
  3. Dashboard (6.2 KB gz) — twelve tiles in width-filling rows (.dashboard-row, a 3:1 top split that collapses without the decision queue); one query per report shared across tiles; every tile owns its skeleton, refusal and As at footer; null renders as Unavailable.
  4. Reports (6.1 KB gz) — period presets and custom dates, previous-period comparison on every headline and per location, revenue by day / week / weekday, sales per day, ranked locations, cash and credit split, gross margin / inventory days / distribution by location and group, stock on hand, haulage by carrier; CSV export per table.
  5. Chart primitives (hand-rolled SVG, ui/charts) — DailyBars, Columns, SplitBars, Bars (with withheld rows and a target mark), Meter, Sparkline, and scale.ts, the one place a bigint becomes a pixel.
  6. Client-side arithmetic — features/office/aggregate.ts: week and weekday buckets that sum exactly, explicit half-up averages, basis-point changes that are null against nothing, top-N with an "others" fold, RFC 4180 CSV. Money-category tests.
  7. Server — reports.salesByDay: a zero row for every day, Σ(days)=total checked at runtime, 400-day cap; money-identity and two-tenant isolation tests.
  8. Money display — <Money grouped> groups thousands for reading, applied after the canonical formatter, which stays ungrouped and parseable.
  9. Next — data the design is ahead of: a tenant-wide credit exposure query (the credit book stat and exposure-vs-limit bullets); gross margin by category; deliveries on the dashboard; the tenant's display name synced to the device; plan targets as tenant configuration so a "vs plan" pill and plan line can exist without typing the financial model into code; sales by hour (needs the sale's business time in the report).
